newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian nurse's family rejects mercy for accused.
newsitem.headline: Australian nurse's family rejects mercy for accused.

text.p: The brother of an Australian nurse murdered in Saudi Arabia was quoted on Monday as saying her family would not ask for clemency for two British nurses accused of her killing and facing beheading under Islamic law.
"My sister was not shown any mercy when she was murdered," said Frank Gilford, from the small farming town of Jamestown north of Adelaide.
"Let the laws of the land deal with the case," he told local media. "The Bible says an eye for an eye."
Gilford's sister Yvonne, 55, was stabbed four times, battered with a hammer and smothered in her dormitory at the King Fahd military medical complex in Dhahran on December 11.
British nurses Lucille McLauchlan, 31, and Deborah Parry, 41, have been charged with murder, but have withdrawn confessions, their lawyer said on Sunday.
The two women, who could face public beheading if found guilty, have said police had promised they would be sent home if they confessed.
Gilford said he did not feel any sympathy for the women and would not intervene, even if approached directly by their families.
"If they were to call me, I would ask them how they would feel if this happened to them," he said.
"It's happened to my sister and to mum's daughter, and I would not be asking the authorities for leniency. No way."

The penalty for murder in Saudi Arabia under Islamic sharia law is beheading, but the sentence can be commuted at the request of the victim's family which can also ask for financial settlement or blood money instead of the death penalty.
Gilford said he had not been contacted by defence lawyers or Saudi officials over the matter.
